extracted.intended_audience: educators, educational theorists, teacher-trainers, and policymakers interested in philosophy of education and vocational training
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative criteria for organizing education with respect to individuality, freedom, and vocation — especially the role of occupations and vocational aims in schooling. Emphasizes how different philosophical stances translate into educational practice and the requirements for effective vocational training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority theory / authoritative education
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational practice that emphasizes the authority of book and teacher and treats deviations and departures as evidence of disturbance or corruption in the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a method tolerates individual intellectualism only in narrow technical regions (mathematics, physics, astronomy) but denies its applicability to morals, social, legal, and political matters; it puts stress on dogma and eternal truths 'made known by revelation, intuition, or the wisdom of our forefathers', discouraging individual variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationalism / abstract intellectualism
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal logical faculty set up in distinction from tradition and concrete subject matter, relying on general impersonal forms of reason to secure external consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has merits in undermining prejudice and promoting clarity and order, but is 'formal and empty' when conceived apart from subject matter; in education it correlates with 'trust in general ready-made rules and principles to secure agreement' and is insufficient for generating new associations, aims, or methods because it disregards habit, instinct, and emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilitarian/self-interest approach (English tradition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal to intelligent self-interest and institutional arrangements (law, penal administration, trade) to align individual actions with social ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes recognition of value in labor and contributes to democratic social concern by showing how private pursuit (trade) can contribute to others' welfare, but is 'tainted by the narrowness of its fundamental premise' that individuals act only from regard for their own pleasures and pains, leading to a 'cash nexus' conception and educational equivalents of reward/penalty systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional idealism / state-centered education
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy that conceives reason as absolute and social institutions (the state) as the incarnation of organized reason, making individual rationality a matter of absorbing social content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages nationally organized education and organized efficiency, sanctions freedom of inquiry in technical details, but tends to reinstate authority in ultimate moral matters and makes little provision for experimental modification of social organization; political democracy is 'foreign to it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom as an intellectual attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom designates a mental attitude: 'intellectual initiative, independence in observation, judicious invention, foresight of consequences, and ingenuity of adaptation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom should be secured by conditions that enable individuals to 'make his own special contribution to a group interest' and to partake of activities such that social guidance is a matter of his own mental attitude rather than authoritative dictation; focus on conditions conducive to effective thinking rather than mere physical unconstraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for physical activity in learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The play of individuality (freedom) cannot be separated from opportunity for free play of physical movements; enforced physical quietude may be unfavorable to realization of a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-activity includes investigation, experimentation, trying out ideas upon things, and discovering what can be done with materials and appliances; schooling must allow a judicious amount of overt physical activity compatible with stages of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-activity and experiential learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-activity is the educative process involving overt experimentation and application, not merely internal reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too often 'self-activity' has been restricted to something internal and excluding physical activity; genuine self-activity demands opportunities to test suggestions, perform experiments, and engage with materials so that learning through doing takes place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of individual and social learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual activity and group association are complementary; certain capacities manifest only under the stimulus of associating with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual work (being let alone) is necessary for calm and concentration but should be balanced with group activities because social interaction stimulates capacities; individuality should not be equated with mere spatial isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for individuality (double meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuality means (1) having one's own purpose and problem (thinking for oneself) and (2) variations in point of view, appeal of objects, and modes of attack from person to person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education must allow pupils to have their own purposes, to observe, reflect, frame and test suggestions; suppressing these variations by enforcing a single mold of study causes loss of originality, confidence, and promotes docility or unregulated idea proliferation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of attitude over product
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational value should be placed on 'originality of attitude' — the unforced personal response of a learner — rather than on originality as measured by product or discovery at advanced levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While young pupils will not make discoveries from the standpoint of experts, they can make genuine discoveries relative to their standpoint; educators should expect learning conditions that permit learners' discoveries rather than demanding adult-level originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of uniform molds and mechanical reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring pupils to reproduce material in the exact form conceived by older persons suppresses instinctive originality and renders teaching and learning conventional and mechanical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should avoid holding pupils to rehearsing material verbatim; doing so denies useful individual variations and prevents teachers from gaining new points of view through intellectual companionship with pupils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation balances individual aptitude and social service
rubrics_metrics.description: An occupation is the means by which an individual's distinctive capacities are matched with social service; 'To find out what one is fitted to do and to secure an opportunity to do it is the key to happiness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right occupation means aptitudes are in adequate play with minimal friction and maximum satisfaction; society benefits when individuals are engaged where they give the best service they can render.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocation as an organizing principle for knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A vocation provides an axis which orders an immense diversity of detail, causing facts and information relevant to the calling to be noted and related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a vocation is tied to needs and results, it attracts and retains relevant information more solidly than abstract, consciously arranged classifications; vocation-motivated organization of knowledge is dynamic and practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training through occupations (learning by doing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only adequate training for occupations is training through occupations: engaging in those active occupations indicated by the pupil's needs and interests rather than purely abstract preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should make earlier preparation indirect rather than direct for specific future jobs; engaging pupils in presently meaningful occupations supports discovery of aptitudes and develops alert observation, coherent planning, and intellectual reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rigid early specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Predetermining a specific future occupation for a pupil ('definitive, irretrievable, and complete choice') injures present development and reduces adequacy of later preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vocational guidance should permit discovery to be continuous; a rough sketch of a future calling is acceptable, but educators should avoid locking students into narrow, fossilizing specialisms that hamper future readjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocational multiplicity (people have multiple callings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conceive vocation as one exclusive calling; individuals necessarily have a variety of callings, each of which should be intelligently developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overemphasizing one specialized phase to the exclusion of others leads to a diminished human development; education should account for diverse roles (family, business, citizenship, artistry) rather than single-track training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of limiting vocation by class or economic coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: When vocations are restricted by social class or economic systems (e.g., slavery or imposed apprenticeship), much talent remains unavailable and society suffers loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems that confine individuals to prescribed callings reduce stimulus, waste talent, and hamper both individual development and societal wellbeing; democratic education should counteract such restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust education to changing social valuation of vocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Because industrial and commercial vocations have grown in social importance, education must reconsider its relation to industrial life and the preparation it offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent increases in the importance of manufacturing and commerce require schools to face new problems of relating schooling to industrial life; democratic esteem for manual labor and service argues for explicit vocational implications in education.
